kf1.tip: Say what would go wrong if croissants were made with a fat that lacks plasticity, first in a cold kitchen and then in a warm one.
kf1.note: A strong answer splits the two kitchens. In a cold kitchen, a fat that lacks plasticity would crumble and break through the dough layers. In a warm one, it would melt into the dough. Either way the separate layers that make a croissant are destroyed. Most people conclude that plasticity matters because the fat must stay solid in layers yet roll and fold without cracking. If you only wrote "the croissant would be flat" without mentioning layers, the reasoning is missing.

kf2.tip: Pick a bake you like and say which raising agents it uses (chemical, mechanical, steam or biological) and how each one makes it rise.
kf2.note: A good answer names the bake, names each raising agent it uses, and says what gas each one makes and how. Chemical agents release carbon dioxide when moisture and heat are applied. Mechanical methods such as creaming or whisking trap air. Steam forms when water in the mixture reaches 100°C. Yeast makes carbon dioxide by fermentation. Check you explained how the gas makes the bake rise, not just listed agents. Many bakes use more than one, and any moist mixture produces some steam.

cs1.tip: Argue for and against storing cut apple in an airtight container, using enzymic browning and vitamin C oxidation, then decide.
cs1.note: A strong answer weighs both reactions separately. For: an airtight container slows the oxidation that destroys vitamin C. Against: it will not prevent enzymic browning once cutting has released polyphenol oxidase. Most decide that a container alone is not enough. Acid such as lemon juice is what stops the browning, though it does not protect vitamin C, so using both makes sense. The trap is treating them as one process and claiming sealing the apple stops it going brown.
